data.title: Amazon Prime Big Deal Days in October drove $9.86 billion in online spending, Adobe says
data.description:
Amazon Prime Big Deal Days returned on Oct. 6 and 7 in 2026, and data published by Adobe shows that shoppers spent more than when the event was held on Oct. 7 and 8 in 2025.

The two-day sales event, which fell on a Tuesday and Wednesday in both years, saw online shoppers spend $9.86 billion at U.S. retailers in its latest iteration, according to Adobe analysts. Adobe’s data is based on direct transactions online, including more than 1 trillion visits to U.S. retail sites, 100 million SKUs and 18 product categories, according to the company.

More than 200 of the Top 2000 largest online retailers used Adobe for web analytics in 2025. They combined for more than $836 billion in ecommerce sales that year.

Amazon ranks No. 1 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 2000 Database. The database is how Digital Commerce 360 tracks the largest North American online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Amazon is also No. 3 in Digital Commerce 360’s Global Online Marketplaces Database. That database ranks the 100 largest such marketplaces by third-party gross merchandise value (GMV).

How much did consumers spend during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days in October?

Online sales at U.S. retailers increased 8.5% year over year while Amazon Prime Big Deal Days was going on in 2026. As the total, $9.86 billion, grew, so did the rate of increase. In 2025, sales were up 7.3% to reach $9.09 billion.

Adobe sees this activity leading retailers to invest in earlier pre-holiday promotions than they would otherwise hold.

Those discounts reached a peak of 20% off listed price, according to Adobe. As they did, the deepest discounts appeared in merchandise categories including computers, televisions, electronics, toys and apparel.

Among these categories, electronics sales spiked, up by 85% from average sales levels in September 2026, Adobe assessed. Meanwhile, toy sales increased by 158%, and video game sales were up 90%. Sales in the personal care products category were up 73% from September.

In electronics specifically, sales of products such as headphones and speakers were up 300% from September, with smartwatch sales up 255%, camera sales up 135% and smartphone sales up 130%. In the meantime, ahead of Halloween, costume sales increased by 610% and candy sales grew by 180%, Adobe reported.

How shoppers made purchases during Prime Big Deal Days in October

Adobe also tracked how online shoppers made purchases over the two-day sales period, noting that purchases made on mobile devices made up 52.0% of all online sales, roughly $5.1 billion and up 12.8% year over year.

In many cases, buy now, pay later (BNPL) services saw heavy use as well. Adobe credited BNPL with enabling 6.0% of online orders over the two days, giving those options a role in $692.3 million in sales. That total was up 4.0% from October’s Prime event 2025.

Looking ahead, Adobe projects that BNPL will drive more than $1 billion in spending on Cyber Monday, which falls on Nov. 30 in 2026.

data.title: Target kicks off holiday season with interactive toy catalog and digital wish lists
data.description:
Target started a major holiday season push on Monday with its new interactive Holiday Kids Catalog, presenting toys in colorful, interactive contexts. The retailer positioned the release as a discovery tool including video content, wish lists and a feature that converts handwritten wish lists into digital shopping lists.

The catalog is available on Target.com and in the retailer’s app. It features nearly 500 toys, games and gifts. However, it is distinct from Target’s separate, curated toy list.

Target is No. 5 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database, which ranks North America’s largest online retailers by annual ecommerce sales.

Target is also No. 54 in Digital Commerce 360’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

What’s new in Target’s toy catalog experience

The catalog is designed to function like a shoppable content platform rather than a product grid, according to Target. Shoppers can watch toy demonstrations and video reviews and add items directly to a cart or save them to a wish list. Wish lists can be shared with family members and gift-givers.

In addition, Target implemented a list scanner feature, which allows shoppers who receive or create a handwritten wish list from the printed catalog to scan it in the Target app and convert it into a digital list. Each page of the physical catalog also carries a unique QR code that links directly to the corresponding page in the digital version.

“This year’s digital experience helps families discover toys together, create and share wish lists and find gifts they’ll be excited about all season long,” said Cassandra Jones, senior vice president, Fun101, Target.

Target’s competition with Amazon

Amazon launched its own Holiday Kids Gift Book on the same day as Target’s announcement on Oct. 5.  Now in its ninth year, Amazon’s version features more than 600 toys and gifts, an original illustrated story and family activity pages. 

While Target’s experience is app-native and built around social sharing and creator content, Amazon’s selling point is Alexa integration. Families can unlock a choose-your-own-adventure audio experience through a partnership with Readyland, with kids interacting with the book’s Forest Friends characters via any Alexa-enabled device.

Amazon’s book also comes with its own curated list of top toys chosen by an in-house team of toy experts alongside AI shopping tools. Alexa for Shopping lets parents make requests like “holiday gifts for my 10-year-old daughter” and receive personalized recommendations based on follow-up questions about interests and hobbies. Amazon Lens allows shoppers to scan a product spotted in person or on social media and find it immediately on Amazon.

Amazon ranks No. 1 in the Top 1000 database.

The state of ecommerce at Target

Target’s online sales grew 8.7% year over year in its fiscal Q2 2026, outpacing total comparable sales growth of 3.8%. Same-day delivery drove more than 25% growth in the quarter, and Target fulfilled about 30% more same- and next-day units year over year.

Total net sales in Q2 increased 5.3% to $26.7 billion, though the quarter’s results were boosted by nearly $1 billion in tariff refunds that Target recorded as a reduction to cost of sales. 

The company’s Fun101 category, which covers toys, sporting goods and entertainment, reported double-digit comparable sales growth in Q2, making it the strongest-performing category of the quarter.

data.title: Ikea, Kodiak prepare to launch driverless freight service in Texas
data.description:
After four years of testing autonomous freight with a safety driver behind the wheel, Ikea is preparing to go fully driverless in Texas using Kodiak’s autonomous driving technology.

Later this year, the Sweden-based home furnishings retailer plans to launch driverless service with Kodiak on a roughly 220-mile stretch connecting the Houston and Dallas metro areas. The highway leg is part of a nearly 300-mile delivery route moving Ikea goods from its Baytown distribution center to its store in Frisco.

“IKEA has been a wonderful partner and customer for four years, and this represents the next chapter,” Don Burnette, Kodiak’s founder and CEO, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Sept. 29.

Originally intended as a three-month trial, the pilot between Ikea and Kodiak continued for four years. During that span, Kodiak said its trucks carried more than 1,300 Ikea loads and logged more than 750,000 autonomous miles. The company described the service as operating “without incident” and with a “nearly perfect” on-time delivery record.

The launch comes as autonomous freight moves beyond small-scale pilots and into day-to-day operations. Walmart, Kroger and Loblaw have all tested or deployed autonomous vehicles for middle-mile deliveries, while PepsiCo said it’s expanding driverless freight across several states.

Ikea ranks No. 6 in the Europe Database, Digital Commerce 360’s ranking of the largest online retailers in the region by their annual ecommerce sales. There, Digital Commerce 360 categorizes it as a Housewares & Home Furnishings retailer.

How Kodiak is preparing for driverless freight

In a Sept. 29 update, Kodiak said it has hauled Ikea goods along the Texas route day and night, seven days a week, and through varying weather conditions. Later this year, Ikea will become Kodiak’s launch shipper for driverless long-haul highway service, with no safety driver aboard.

Kodiak provides the autonomous driving system behind the trucks. Its core product, the Kodiak Driver, combines AI-powered software with modular hardware installed on commercial vehicles. The company offers the technology through a Driver-as-a-Service model and strategic partnerships.

Before it removes safety drivers, Kodiak is also completing its final round of testing. In a Sept. 25 release, the company shared that its trucks have been making deliveries between its Lancaster, Texas, hub and Houston since August without the driver taking control, including on surface streets. Kodiak said it’s also running closed-course tests to recreate situations “that occur too rarely, or are too risky, to test on public highways.”

“Our progress since beginning our final push towards driverless commercial deliveries has been incredible, and it is a strong signal we are ready to scale unsupervised driverless service on long-haul lanes,” Burnette said in the Sept. 25 release.

Kodiak already operates without drivers in another setting. Since December 2024, Atlas Energy Solutions has used customer-owned trucks equipped with the Kodiak Driver to haul freight in the Permian Basin of West Texas and eastern New Mexico. As of June, Kodiak reported that 35 Atlas trucks using the system had logged more than 40,000 hours of paid driverless operations.

What driverless freight could mean for Ikea

With Ikea, Kodiak is taking that technology from an industrial setting to a major interstate freight lane. The company said four years of testing also taught it how to integrate autonomous trucks into Ikea’s supply chain, from scheduling departures and unloading docks to using vehicle data for predictive maintenance.

“We now know exactly what it takes to transform the underlying technology into an AI-driven product that generates value and efficiency,” Kodiak said in its Sept. 29 blog post.

Ikea has already seen some of those potential benefits elsewhere. After testing, Ikea China permanently adopted self-driving electric vehicles at its Hefei operation, Ingka Group said in March. Ingka is Ikea’s largest franchisee and operates its U.S. retail business, including 61 retail locations.

The vehicles move goods between a warehouse and the store for customer pickup orders and restocking. During the test, the trucks traveled nearly 75,600 kilometers, or about 47,000 miles, according to Ingka. The company said they cut average wait times for pickup orders from six hours to two. Transportation costs between Ikea locations also fell by more than 50%.

Ikea is also testing autonomous deliveries directly to customers in China. Ingka said it is evaluating whether the Hefei model could work in other markets where regulations and infrastructure allow.

Other companies expand driverless freight

Retailers and consumer brands are increasingly using autonomous trucks for middle-mile routes.

Walmart was an early adopter. In 2021, the retailer and autonomous trucking company Gatik removed the safety driver from box trucks running a roughly 7-mile route between a Walmart facility and a neighborhood market in Bentonville, Arkansas. According to Gatik, it was “the first time an autonomous trucking company has removed the safety driver from a commercial delivery route on the middle mile.”

More recently, in June, PepsiCo signed a multiyear agreement with Gatik to expand autonomous freight across its North American supply chain. Driverless trucks are already operating for PepsiCo in Texas, Arizona and Arkansas. FreightWaves reported that the network serves about 250 retail locations, including Walmart and Dollar General stores. Walmart ranks No. 2 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales. Dollar General is ranked No. 674 in the Top 1000.

Meanwhile, the economics of autonomous trucking may depend heavily on distance and scale. A 2026 study by researchers at North Dakota State University estimated potential savings of about 13% for a 200-mile hub-to-hub route, rising to 31% at 1,000 miles when fleets reach sufficient scale.

Without that scale, shorter autonomous routes could cost more, they found. The study did not examine Ikea, but its roughly 220-mile driverless leg is close to the shorter route modeled.

data.title: TD Synnex, Siemens partner to expand industrial AI and IT-OT distribution globally
data.description:
TD Synnex and Siemens are set to collaborate internationally as the two companies partner on distribution.

Combining TD Synnex’s information technology offerings and Siemens’ own infrastructure and automation portfolio, the companies announced their agreement with their eyes on industrial use cases for artificial intelligence.

Together, they plan to meet demand for software and physical AI, according to Siemens.

Why TD Synnex and Siemens are working together

“With the incredible pace of change driven by AI, bringing IT and OT [operational technology] closer together has never been more important,” said Alastair Borissow, head of global distribution sales at Siemens. “By combining our established and highly capable global OT distribution network with TD Synnex’s complementary strengths in IT distribution, scale and ecosystem we intend to create new opportunities for our entire distribution channel.”

The Oct. 5 joint announcements noted that TD Synnex and Siemens agreed on a “joint framework” that would enable their global partnership. They highlighted Siemens’ technology and TD Synnex’s expertise and customer outcomes.

“IT and OT convergence is creating significant opportunities for partners to connect enterprise technology with the systems that power industries, infrastructure and buildings,” said Cheryl Day, senior vice president, new vendor acquisition and global solutions at TD Synnex. “By combining Siemens’ industrial technology expertise with TD Synnex’s global partner ecosystem, enablement capabilities and value-added services, we can help partners access new markets, develop new skills and address emerging opportunities in areas such as industrial AI, automation, cybersecurity and digital infrastructure.”

What TD Synnex and Siemens hope to achieve

“This is about far more than the distribution of technology — it is about connecting the industrial and IT worlds at unprecedented scale — by combining Siemens’ deep industrial technology with TD Synnex’s extraordinary reach across the global IT ecosystem — from hyperscalers and technology providers to thousands of specialist partners,” said Dion Smith, head of global partner ecosystem at Siemens. “We aim to create new routes to market, engage new buying centers within existing customers and reach entirely new customers, while accelerating the convergence of IT and OT.”

Smith noted the potential market that TD Synnex and Siemens could address through their combined efforts. In his view, the opportunity could be worth as much as $1 trillion. TD Synnex already operates across more than 100 countries, according to the distributor. If they are successful, Smith sees the partnership as a path to improve their reach.

“Together, we have the opportunity to unlock a trillion-dollar market and make secure industrial digitalization more accessible, scalable and impactful worldwide,” Smith stated.

data.title: Revelyst brands focus on discovery, understanding AI traffic
data.description:
Revelyst, which operates more than a dozen brands for outdoor recreation and related gear, has seen a rise in artificial intelligence-driven product discovery in 2026 — and it’s working to uncover what consumers are using AI platforms to understand about its products.

Consumers are learning more about Revelyst’s products outside of its brand sites, according to Tari Huddleston, global vice president of digital and ecommerce. Consumers are engaging with various AI tools — which can include ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity — to understand Revelyst products’ features and specifications.

“We’re seeing what the questions are that are being asked around our brand,” Huddleston told Digital Commerce 360. “Either their features or questions about the technology, the innovation that’s inside it. We’re watching that and seeing how that has changed. It’s not all transactional based anymore.”

Revelyst operates brands including:

  • Bell
  • Blackhawk
  • Blackburn
  • Bushnell
  • Bushnell Golf
  • CamelBak (No. 1,212 in the Top 2000 Database)
  • Camp Chef (No. 965 in the Top 2000)
  • Foresight Sports
  • Fox Racing
  • Giro
  • Primos
  • Quietkat
  • Simms
  • Stone Glacier

The Top 2000 Database ranks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Camp Chef is also No. 571 in Digital Commerce 360’s new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

AI discovery trends among Revelyst brands

Although Huddleston did not share specific metrics regarding AI referral traffic, she noted that her brands have seen comparable trends to other retailers Digital Commerce 360 has spoken with.

That is, retailers in early 2026 have seen about 1% to 3% of website traffic come from AI referrals. In the second half of 2026, that has risen to about 4% to 7%, but certainly less than 10% for those retailers.

Within that AI traffic subset, Huddleston noted, consumers shopping Revelyst brands are adding products to their carts more than their counterparts. The AI responses to their queries are leading them directly to product detail pages (PDPs) rather than homepages.

Such AI tools are helping consumers to complete the top-of-funnel product discovery, she said. That refers to the earliest stage of a consumer learning about a brand or its products.

“They’re ready to convert,” Huddleston said. “We’re seeing that they’ve done that homework and they’re ready to make that purchase.”

What consumers are using AI to understand about products

The rates of AI referrals to Revelyst brand sites are comparable to one another. AI traffic referrals are increasing among Revelyst brands, but they’re still small, according to Huddleston. She noted that “many other channels” are driving the majority of her brands’ traffic.

“I think the reason why it’s still small is because the discovery phase for the consumer, for our products, is not a short window,” Huddleston explained. “It’s not like someone’s deciding: Hey, I need a replacement of something — which is a quick purchase.”

Instead, it’s often a long-term investment, she said. Huddleston gave the example that a consumer shopping for a power sports helmet could be looking at a price range of $400 to $900 — “a sizable investment.”

That type of purchase often requires more research than smaller-ticket items. As a result, consumers are asking more questions about products to decide if they’re worth the price. Huddleston said Revelyst uses those questions to determine how it can improve its PDPs.

Another example was of a consumer asking about pads inside of a helmet and how speakers factored in.

“We would not have known that that was a feature that we need to call out and be able to make sure was searchable across the product unless we had been watching and seeing what type of conversations were happening inside the space,” Huddleston said.
